frameworks.name: Obliquity Framework
frameworks.definition: Problems that have not yielded to logical solutions are precisely those that require counterintuitive, oblique, or tangential approaches; logical problems have mostly already been solved.

frameworks.name: Centaur Theory (Human + AI)
frameworks.definition: The optimal intelligent agent is a human plus a machine working together; the best chess player is not a machine but a human-machine pair, and this principle scales to everyday knowledge work.

frameworks.name: Georgist Land Value Tax
frameworks.definition: A taxation framework in which only the unimproved value of land is taxed (not labor or capital improvements), on the grounds that land value is created by collective action rather than individual effort, making its appreciation a form of rent-seeking rather than earned return.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that logical solutions to persistent problems are exhausted by definition: if a problem could be solved by straightforward reasoning, the large supply of logical people in the world would already have solved it. Therefore the problems that remain are precisely those that require counterintuitive, oblique, or tangential thinking.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: By a kind of Darwinian selection, problems that yield to logic are eliminated over time by the abundance of logical thinkers, leaving only problems that require non-logical approaches.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that listening to a podcast conversation is epistemically equivalent to the Platonic dialogue tradition, and may be epistemically superior to reading a philosophy book, because philosophical inquiry is supposed to proceed through live conversation rather than through a pre-planned written argument.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: applies to open-ended philosophical or discovery-oriented content
not applicable to reference works or technical manuals
claims.mechanism: Written philosophy is a simulacrum of the ideal process; conversation allows trial and error in ideas, which the philosophical process requires.
bounded_by: Does not apply where reference or precision is required (e.g. technical documentation)

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that a human information intermediary who is highly skilled at navigating AI tools and digital interfaces is more economically valuable per user than direct unmediated AI access, because the human can resolve alignment failures (where the algorithm does not know what the user actually wants), exercise contextual judgment, and maintain the trust relationship that low-trust digital systems cannot replicate.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: applies to high-complexity, ambiguous, or trust-sensitive queries
applies where the human is shared across many clients (20 minutes per client per day)
claims.mechanism: Algorithms are calibrated for very low levels of trust and cannot perform contextual benefit-of-the-doubt reasoning; a skilled human-AI pair resolves this alignment gap and can be distributed across ~100 clients at economically sustainable cost.
bounded_by: Does not apply to fully specified, routine transactions where the user knows exactly what they want

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that Quaker commercial culture was extraordinarily efficient because trust between parties eliminated the need for legal intermediaries (lawyers, oath-taking, contract enforcement), enabling deals to close on a handshake. This allowed Quakers -- a tiny population -- to found disproportionately many major British commercial institutions including Cadbury, Rowntree, Barclays Bank, and Lloyds Bank.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: applies to communities with high mutual trust and reputational stakes
Quaker example is 17th-19th century British commerce
claims.mechanism: When every statement a party makes carries the force of sworn truth (Quaker principle: no need for oaths), transaction costs collapse because trust-creating intermediaries become unnecessary.
bounded_by: Fails in low-trust or anonymous markets where reputation enforcement is absent

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that UK and US property price rises are good news for only a very small group -- those with parents planning to die soon, or those planning to downsize -- and bad news for everyone else (non-owners, upsizers, those with no prospect of inheritance). The dominant media framing of property price rises as universally good news is a form of collective insanity.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: applies to primary-residence real estate in markets where ownership is the dominant wealth-storage vehicle (UK, US)
bounded_by: In markets where housing is primarily rented (Germany) the claim structure is different
Does not apply to investment-only property portfolios

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that land value appreciation is a form of rent-seeking that should be heavily taxed, because the value of land is created by collective action (government road-building, planning permission, monetary policy, community formation) rather than by the individual owner's effort or investment. Improvements the owner makes to a building should remain untaxed as those represent earned return.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: applies to land value appreciation created by external collective action
explicitly excludes value created by owner improvements
claims.mechanism: Whenever useful activity depends on location, economic gains flow to the landowner rather than to the performers of the activity -- the owner contributes nothing but captures the surplus.
bounded_by: Does not apply to value created by owner's own improvements or investment

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the planning-permission system in the UK is an absurd wealth transfer: issuing planning permission converts agricultural land worth approximately £3,000-4,000 per acre into land worth potentially £1 million or more per acre near London, yet the state captures almost none of this uplift. Instead it is gifted to the landowner who contributed nothing to create it.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: applies to UK planning system; magnitudes are approximate and Sutherland acknowledges being out of date
greatest uplift in high-demand commuter zones near London
claims.mechanism: Planning permission is a government act that multiplies land value by orders of magnitude; the beneficiary is the landowner, not the government or the neighboring community.

numbers.axis: land value per acre by planning status near London

anchors.region: land with residential planning permission within 20 min of Euston
anchors.value: possibly £1 million or more per acre

bounded_by: Magnitudes are Sutherland's rough estimate and acknowledged as potentially out of date
Differential is smaller in low-demand rural areas

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the double-income household began as an option that improved quality of life but over time became an obligation, because the additional purchasing power was captured largely by the property market (house prices rose to absorb two incomes) and the government (twice the income tax). The net quality-of-life gain for a typical dual-income household was modest while they permanently lost roughly 35 hours of discretionary time per week per household.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: applies to long-run equilibrium across households, not to early adopters of dual income who captured the initial advantage
UK context; Sutherland attributes aligned analysis to Elizabeth Warren and Faye Weldon
claims.mechanism: As dual income became widespread, sellers (property market, government via tax) priced in the new purchasing power, so the surplus that early dual-income households captured was competed away.

numbers.axis: weekly discretionary time lost per household

bounded_by: Early adopters of dual income captured real gains before markets adjusted
Does not apply equally in markets where property is not the dominant savings vehicle

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that consumer electronics (phones, televisions, computers) are not rivalrous consumption -- buying an iPhone makes iPhones cheaper for others -- whereas housing is purely rivalrous consumption: every household that occupies a dwelling deprives another household of it. This distinction, which mainstream economics conflates, makes housing categorically different from other goods and justifies different tax treatment.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Consumer electronics have scale economies and non-excludable knowledge spillovers; land is fixed in supply and location-specific, so occupation is zero-sum.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that purchasing a new car is an act of philanthropy toward poorer consumers: the buyer absorbs the depreciation, so a buyer of the six-year-old car gets a luxury vehicle at a fraction of the original cost. He argues that buying a house in a desirable area has the opposite effect -- it is purely rivalrous and imposes no benefit on others.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Manufactured goods have scale economies and resale markets that transmit quality gains to later buyers; land does not depreciate and cannot be shared.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that entropy continuously pulls systems toward normalcy, and that distinctiveness and profit both require active, ongoing resistance against that gravitational pull. A business or person that stops actively maintaining distinctiveness will regress toward average.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Without active investment, competitive pressures and imitation push offerings toward commodity; distinctiveness is not a state but a continuous effort against mean reversion.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that large-scale protest culture is counterproductive for cause advancement because the most extreme behaviors (purity spirals) are generated for in-group signaling, but when observed by the broader public they tend to set the cause back rather than advance it. He cites Neil Kinnock's 1992 pre-election rally as the canonical example.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: applies to broadcast-era protests where behavior is visible to non-members via media
not applicable to closed in-group signaling with no external audience
claims.mechanism: Groups under social pressure escalate to more extreme behavior to prove group membership; the behavior that maximizes in-group signaling value is also the behavior most likely to alienate the broader audience that the protest seeks to persuade.
bounded_by: Some successful protest movements did achieve goals -- Sutherland notes survivorship bias in belief about protest effectiveness

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that mainstream economics has made a structural error by conflating capital and land as a single category, following from Adam Smith's explicit distinction between the three factors of production (labor, capital, land). Because land value is determined by the actions of others and by the community rather than by the landowner, it cannot and should not be governed by the same rules as capital.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that property -- not labor income -- is the dominant driver of intergenerational wealth inequality in contemporary Britain, and that wealth position is now more a product of when and where one happened to buy a house than of contribution to society. This concentration of wealth in an illiquid, rivalrous, non-productive asset class is, in his view, as dysfunctional as making the national lottery 50% of the economy.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: UK property market context; specific claim about post-quantitative-easing era
bounded_by: Does not apply equally to countries with different land ownership and tax structures (e.g. Germany, Singapore)

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that Google Maps embodies a hidden Californian assumption: users are either pure car-owners (drive everywhere) or car-less (rely on public transport for the full journey). This binary ignores the common British practice of driving to a railway station and taking the train, producing ludicrously pessimistic journey time estimates for public transport options.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: applies specifically to Google Maps public-transport routing in the UK
more accurate for US cities where drive-to-station is uncommon
claims.mechanism: An algorithm trained on US behavioral patterns (especially Los Angeles) where car-ownership is near-total encodes assumptions that generate systematic errors in multi-modal European journey planning.
bounded_by: Google Maps has improved and third-party tools (Trainline) partially solve the split-ticketing problem

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the new opportunities that AI appears to offer look perfect because their costs are invisible -- mastering new interfaces, resolving alignment failures, enduring errors -- while the problems of existing arrangements feel larger than they are. This asymmetry causes systematic undervaluation of human intermediaries relative to AI tools.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Hidden costs of new technology (learning new interfaces, resolving alignment failures) are invisible at decision time, while costs of existing arrangements (hiring a human) are salient, causing people to switch to AI tools even when the human-AI pair is strictly superior.
bounded_by: For fully specified, routine, low-judgment tasks AI tools without a human intermediary are genuinely superior

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that rail-booking algorithms overweight journey time as an optimization criterion, causing slow-but-cheap direct trains to disappear from recommendations and from consumer awareness. He cites the Waterloo-via-Salisbury route to the West Country as a specific case where ignoring the algorithmic recommendation yields dramatically cheaper tickets (first-class singles at a fraction of Paddington fares).
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: applies to UK rail booking websites
example: Waterloo via Salisbury to Exeter/Plymouth vs. Paddington
claims.mechanism: Algorithms optimize for a visible metric (journey time) that is easy to rank, causing slower trains to be systematically suppressed from results and creating underpriced capacity for users who know to search differently.
bounded_by: Availability and pricing of specific routes changes; the general principle may not apply to all slow routes

examples.text: Rory Sutherland describes a scenario on a train where a non-English-speaking woman had boarded the wrong train and was crying because she could not communicate her situation. He helped via Google Translate and eventually a train operator wrote a note on the back of her ticket explaining her situation and asking colleagues not to fine her. Sutherland uses this to illustrate the benefit-of-the-doubt judgment that human intermediaries can exercise and that algorithmic systems are specifically designed not to exercise, because the benefit of the doubt shows up as a financial loss and is vulnerable to fraud in automated systems.

Rory Sutherland gives the example of a widow living in a house worth £2.2 million whose children cannot afford to replace their car's shock absorbers. Before her husband died, the couple would walk home from a restaurant rather than pay a price surcharge that did not apply on Fridays. He uses this to illustrate the extreme illiquidity of housing as wealth storage: the only way to realize the gain is by dying or moving, which means asset-rich households cannot deploy their wealth to improve their own or their families' quality of life.

Rory Sutherland describes a fictional but representative scenario: if buying a Ford Mondeo required also purchasing £200,000 of Ford shares in order to get the car, a buyer would find this absurd -- they just want a car, not a financial instrument. He uses this analogy to argue that property forces buyers to purchase both a place to live and the land rights beneath it, even though the land component is the dominant cost and is entirely rivalrous and unproductive.

Rory Sutherland describes the Caribbean chattel house: a small two-room wooden house, the product of talented carpenters, developed after slavery was abolished in the early 19th century. Freed slaves faced a situation where plantation owners paid wages but reclaimed them as rent. To escape this, workers built portable houses that could be physically moved to whichever plantation offered lower land rent -- thus disentangling housing ownership from land ownership. He uses this as a real-world historical proof that ownership of a dwelling can be separated from ownership of the land on which it stands.

Rory Sutherland describes how Jordan Peterson shifted his university talks from evenings to mornings, and the protests that had previously mobbed his events disappeared overnight because activists could not be bothered to get out of bed early. Sutherland uses this to illustrate his claim that modern protest (now that police cannot practice indiscriminate violence) has become a form of entertainment for a particular social type, rather than a costly signal of conviction.

Rory Sutherland cites the Quaker Oats Company's choice to use a Quaker as their brand image -- despite the company itself having no Quaker connection -- as evidence that Quaker commercial trustworthiness was so historically established that it functioned as a credibility signal even for non-Quaker businesses in the 20th century. The real Quakers (Cadbury, Rowntree, Barclays, Lloyds) founded these institutions precisely because their word-is-bond principle eliminated legal overhead.

practices.text: When booking trains to the West Country (Plymouth, Cornwall), search from Waterloo and add 'via Salisbury' rather than defaulting to Paddington; the Southwestern route is slower, rarely appears in standard results, and is dramatically cheaper including in first class.

To evaluate whether to maintain a large property, apply the car-market analogy: if a house has been occupied for three years it should lose value like a used car. When it does not, the land component -- not the structure -- is maintaining value and the owner is implicitly a land speculator regardless of intent.
